overview: This card follows French-ruled Cochin China in the atlas’s 1920 to 1938 interval, especially Saigon, Cholon and the Mekong delta. It was the southern colony within French Indochina, distinct from the Annam and Tonkin protectorates. The atlas repeats one broad outline across both decades and extends beyond the older Cochin China record. Treat it as approximate coverage, not a surveyed border or a map of one people. Neither 1920 nor 1938 marks the colony’s actual beginning or end.

periods.title: Rice commerce under colonial rule
periods.summary: The southern rice economy connected farmers and mills with export markets, while unequal access to land and credit shaped opportunity.

periods.title: Depression and political organizing
periods.summary: Falling rice prices damaged livelihoods; in Saigon, a new revolutionary newspaper alliance entered municipal politics.

periods.title: A widening public debate
periods.summary: La Lutte gave increasing attention to workers, peasants and the possibilities opened by France’s Popular Front government.

sections.title: Rule, resistance and the rice economy

items.text: Cochin China belonged to the Indochinese Union established in 1887. A French governor ran this directly administered colony, while Annam and Tonkin had separate protectorate administrations. Above them stood the governor-general. These were different layers of colonial authority, not independent Vietnamese governments. Surviving administrative files record decisions about schools, public works, trade, justice and political policing.

In 1933, Vietnamese revolutionaries in Saigon built an unusual alliance around La Lutte, bringing together communists and Trotskyists despite their disagreements. Two associated candidates won municipal seats that May, and four won in 1935. The newspaper helped campaign for workers and political prisoners. Colonial repression had made open organizing dangerous, so using legal journalism and elections was an important tactical change.

The language of a newspaper could affect what its editors were allowed to do. French-language papers operated under different rules from Vietnamese-language ones, which needed advance authorization and faced censorship. La Lutte initially appeared in French even though that sharply limited its audience. A newspaper meant to defend ordinary workers could be difficult for those very workers to read.

Rice connected village labor to distant markets. López Jerez’s study follows prices from producers through Cholon’s milling and trading system to exports. During the Great Depression, prices collapsed between 1929 and 1934. A farming family still had to meet its needs, while falling crop income made debt and tenancy more difficult. Export success did not mean that the gains were shared evenly.

Agricultural research was tied to colonial commercial goals. Provincial stations selected rice seed and multiplied it on experimental plots, hoping to make Cochinchinese rice more competitive in world markets. Officials also promoted fertilizers and farming machinery. These efforts changed technical knowledge about crops, but they served an economy organized heavily around extracting and selling agricultural production.

sections.title: Families, reading and women’s public lives

items.text: In 1928, Phan Thị Bạch Vân established a women’s bookshop in Gò Công. Its reading material ranged from novels and household arts to science, political ideas, maternity and children’s education. A shelf could put family care beside arguments about how society should work. Publishing such ideas carried risks: her work drew prosecution from colonial authorities in 1930.

A women’s fair held in Saigon from 4 to 8 May 1932 promoted products made by women, culinary skills and traditional crafts. It also raised relief funds for flood victims in Nghệ An and supported charitable work. Preparing food or making a craft could become part of public organizing, with women displaying skills, earning attention and helping communities far beyond their own kitchens.

A 1930 newspaper heading reads “Phụ nữ nên tự lập”, translated by the ISEAS Library as “Women should be independent”. It appeared in issue 58 of Saigon’s Phụ Nữ Tân Văn, urging women to build stable careers rather than depend entirely on male relatives. This is Vietnamese in the Latin-based quốc ngữ script, reproduced here in modern type from the library’s transcription. The tone marks are part of the writing.

A 1938 Cholon housing survey drew a comfortable home with an altar, beds, rice jars, a rice pestle and stored drinking water. Poorer families often lived in crowded thatched huts with fewer supplies. In town, shopfronts and living quarters could share a narrow building. Home comfort depended greatly on money and location.

sections.title: Water, toilets, medicine and surviving evidence

items.text: Cholon’s sanitation had a very unglamorous earlier chapter. An 1896 account describes contractors collecting toilet buckets and carrying the contents away. The mayor objected to dumping untreated waste on market gardens and required processing at an outskirts dumping ground. This is background to the interwar city, not proof that every 1930s home used the same arrangement. Keeping a city clean involved much more than sweeping streets.

Interwar Cholon grew unevenly. Poorer districts off Boulevard Galliéni lacked water supply and sewerage, and heavy rain could flood unpaved alleys. Prosperous homes could store drinking water in large containers while poorer ones held less. A new boulevard or tramway therefore did not automatically bring safe water to neighboring families.

Saigon’s Pasteur Institute had been founded in 1891 to bring rabies and smallpox vaccination to Indochina. It was part of the medical infrastructure inherited by the interwar colony. The institute preserves a photograph of its Saigon building in 1930, a physical reminder that laboratories and vaccine work had become part of the city.

The official 1930 statistics counted 1,228 people treated at Saigon’s anti-rabies institute and recorded three deaths. These are administrative treatment figures, not a count of everyone bitten or a measure of universal protection. They show a concrete medical service at work while leaving access outside the clinic uncertain.

Saigon’s Blanchard de la Brosse Museum opened in 1929. Later photographs from 1951 show Khmer stone sculptures and a carved Angkorian lintel among its displays. These objects preserved evidence of older regional societies whose histories were far longer than French rule. The photographs document a later arrangement, so they cannot tell us exactly what an interwar visitor saw.

ending.text: The 1938 atlas cutoff was not Cochin China’s historical fall. Its separate colonial status changed amid the later struggle over Vietnam’s independence. French law of 4 June 1949 attached the territory to the associated State of Vietnam. This did not settle the war or the dispute over sovereignty: contemporary diplomatic records show continued resistance and disagreement over French power. Local communities and their languages continued through these changes in government.
